item.title: Lula’s ‘miracle’ victory buys time for Brazil, resonates globally amid rise of far-right
item.description: The world’s fourth-largest democracy has now bucked the trend of far-right gains, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

item.title: This novel in verse tells the legend of Unniarcha, Kerala’s most fearless Kalaripayattu warrior girl
item.description: An excerpt from ‘I Am Archa’, by Ranjeeta Raam.
item.content:encoded:
Kalaripayattu

is an art.
is warfare.
is a way of living.
is in my blood.
is all I have ever known.
is Kannappa Chekavar.

Kannappa Chekavar

is my acha,
my father.

He is disciplined and strict.
He is loving and encouraging too.

He is also the greatest
Kalari master of Kadathanadu.

He is unmatchable,
unbeatable
in this art of war
fought with every weapon used in close combat.
Wooden staffs, swords, daggers, maces
are mere toys in his hands.

It is said he knows more adavukkal – combat moves –
than anyone else practising Kalaripayattu.
It is also said
that he has never taught
all nineteen of them to anyone.

He has shared all
but the last technique,
the most cunning one,
keeping it close to his heart,
waiting for that special student
worthy enough to earn this secret.

No pity

The consequence of being ten minutes late
is an extra hour of practice.

Breathless and exhausted,
I gaze longingly
at the other students leaving the class.
They must be off to the vacant field
by the village pond
to hang out and play
before the sun sets for the day.

Aromal steps out too,
casting a look of disappointment
in my direction.

Control your breathing, Unniarcha!
Acha interrupts my thoughts.
No pity, no sympathy in that voice.
Sigh!

Agony

Without a word,
I continue practising the chuvadukkal –
the basic steps and foot placements,
into the second hour.

A bout of kicks, squats, lunges and stretches later,
I move on to vadivukkal,
my anger dissipated
like the summer rainstorm outside.

item.title: Centre amends rules to allow E100 fuel in compatible vehicles
item.description: The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on nearly 100% ethanol, alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government has amended rules to allow vehicles designed for flex-fuel to run on E100, a fuel made up of nearly 100% ethanol.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways issued the notification amending the Motor Vehicles Rules on Friday. The changes came into effect on Monday.

The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on E100 alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.

Flex-fuel vehicles can run on different blends of petrol and ethanol. However, regular petrol vehicles, including those designed to run on E20 fuel, which contains 20% ethanol and 80% petrol, cannot use E85 or E100, Hindustan Times reported.

Under its Ethanol Blended Petrol programme, the government mandates that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

An opinion poll by LocalCircles published on July 5 showed that 53% of the surveyed petrol vehicle owners said that they believe that the government’s handling of the E20 rollout was “disastrous” or “ineffective”.

item.title: Seven foreigners in terror-related probe get bail yet Indian undertrials struggle to access rights
item.description: The broader concern is the protections in law are unevenly accessible.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi Special Court’s decision to allow seven foreign nationals under National Investigation Agency investigation in a terrorism-related case to travel home for a month raises a constitutional question: how should criminal law balance national security, investigative deadlines and personal liberty?

The accused, an American national, Matthew Aaron VanDyke and six Ukrainian citizens were arrested in March 2026. The allegations included drone assembly, electronic warfare training and support to ethnic armed organisations along the Indo-Myanmar border.

However, after the statutory period for filing a chargesheet expired, the NIA’s report omitted substantive charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, and instead cited regulatory violations under the Foreigners Act, 1946. The agency maintained that its wider investigation into scheduled terrorism offences continued.

The Special Court for the NIA at Rouse Avenue, New Delhi, granted default bail and later allowed the accused to travel abroad, subject to personal bonds and diplomatic undertakings. They did not decide the merits of the allegations or represent judicial leniency; they enforced a statutory deadline. The central question is not why these foreign nationals secured release, but why comparable safeguards remain difficult for many Indian undertrials to exercise.

Several students of Jamia Millia Islamia university in Delhi were detained by the police on Monday as protests continued on the campus to demand time-bound elections to the students’ union, reported Hindustan Times.

The university has not held student union elections since 2006. Students have been protesting on the campus since October 12, with five of them going on hunger strike, to demand the restoration of their union.

On October 16, the university rusticated one of the students on hunger strike, suspended two and banned all three from entering the campus for a year.

Earlier on Monday, the university administration announced that student union elections would be held within 15 days of the union’s constitution being approved.

The administration also revoked suspension and show-cause notices issued to students during the protest and said a committee would be formed to investigate the conduct of security personnel during the agitation.

item.title: Fiction: A devil with literary aspirations takes up residence within the super devout Kunjamma
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Haunting of Kunjamma P’, by Shinie Antony.
item.content:encoded:
Kunjamma walked briskly down the cemetery to sing oppees loudly and tunelessly at the graves; she chose one headstone each morning, so that no one felt left out when she broke into the Office for the Dead. “Kahla nadam kelkumbol mritharil jeevan udikinnu” was her blithe reassurance to them despite never having died herself. Then, as she could never stop herself from doing this, she peeped into the small dry well in the corner of the cemetery where bones from emptied graves were dumped.

Family tomb plots were sold here, to take in as many corpses the family could provide. But for those who could not prebook a final resting place, a rota system applied. item.title: Voters will not face prosecution for submitting Form 6 after being deleted during SIR, says SC
item.description: The petitioner had submitted that ‘pre-existing voters misrepresenting themselves as fresh voters is an offence’.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday verbally assured that voters would not face prosecution for submitting Form 6 to restore their names to the electoral roll after being excluded during the special intensive revision, Live Law reported.

Form 6 is meant for first-time voter registration. It requires applicants to state that they have not registered or voted previously.

The court was hearing a petition challenging the revision of voter rolls in Maharashtra.

“Pre-existing voters misrepresenting themselves as fresh voters is an offence and liable for prosecution,” the petitioner’s advocate was quoted as saying by Live Law.

In response, Chief Justice Surya Kant said: “Do not worry. Nobody will be prosecuted.”

The court also issued notice to the Election Commission, while refusing to pass an interim order extending the deadline for filing claims and objections or restraining the poll panel from publishing the final electoral roll.

The petitioner had told the court that nearly three crore of Maharashtra’s approximately nine crore voters had been deleted after the draft electoral rolls were published, Live Law reported.

item.title: Karnataka poll officials sought deletions of 61,000 voters without citing reasons: ‘The Hindu’
item.description: The officials said that the Form 7 applications were ‘auto-generated’ with their digital signatures amid the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.
item.content:encoded:
Election officials filed 61,059 Form 7 applications seeking to remove voters from Karnataka’s electoral rolls without stating any reason during the special intensive revision, The Hindu reported on Monday.

The 1960 Registration of Electors Rules mandate that an application to delete voters should be rejected if it does not state the reason for the request.

In the case of Karnataka, electoral registration officers and assistant electoral registration officers said that the system “auto-generated” these forms and added their digital signatures when voters could not be reached during hearings of notices issued for no mapping or “logical discrepancies”, reported The Hindu.

In such cases, voters were marked as “ineligible”.

“Logical discrepancies” flagged by the poll panel during the voter list revision included mismatches in parents’ names, low age gap with parents and the number of children of the parents being above six.

The officials said that they had been instructed to file Form 7 applications if a voter had moved, had a duplicate entry elsewhere, was underage, had died or was not an Indian citizen, The Hindu reported. However, since the forms were auto-generated, the reason for seeking deletion was left blank.

item.title: ‘Long before we named the gods, we painted animals’: There’s a new book of Raghu Rai’s animal photos
item.description: An excerpt from Maneka Gandhi’s Introduction to ‘Animals’, by Raghu Rai.
item.content:encoded:
I have known Raghu Rai for more than half a century. Throughout this time, I have followed his work closely and have been privileged to witness in it his remarkable ability to see what most of us tend to miss. The prowess to take himself seriously and trust his eyes, his sense of humour and the enormous empathy for his subjects – all of these qualities show up in so many of his photographs. But perhaps, they are realised most poignantly in his vast archives of images of animals he has met and lensed during his travels across the country. When I looked through these evocative images, it became clear to me instantly that we had to make them accessible to the world. Each one was a statement.

item.title: Rahul Gandhi acquitted in 2018 defamation case over remarks about Amit Shah
item.description: The Congress leader’s statement that the home minister was a ‘murder accused’ was not defamatory, the court held.
item.content:encoded:
A court in Uttar Pradesh’s Sultanpur on Monday acquitted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi in a criminal defamation case over his 2018 remarks referring to Union Home Minister Amit Shah as a “murder accused”, Bar and Bench reported.

Gandhi was present in court when Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Shubham Verma pronounced the verdict. The court said the remarks were not defamatory in nature.

The case was filed in August 2018 on a complaint by Bharatiya Janata Party leader Vijay Mishra, who alleged that Gandhi had made objectionable remarks about Shah at a press conference in Bengaluru on May 8, 2018, during the Karnataka elections. Shah was the BJP’s national president at the time.

Gandhi had said that the BJP claimed to believe in clean politics but had a party president who was a “murder accused”, in an apparent reference to the 2005 Sohrabuddin Sheikh case.

Sohrabuddin Sheikh, who was a wanted criminal, was killed by the Gujarat Police in November 2005 in an “encounter”, which is alleged to have been staged. He and his wife were travelling by bus from Hyderabad to Sangli in Maharashtra when they were stopped by the Gujarat and Rajasthan police, allegedly abducted and shot dead near Gandhinagar.

item.title: Rahul Gandhi’s convoy meets with accident in UP, Congress leader unhurt
item.description: The leader of Opposition was on way to Sultanpur to appear before a special court in connection with a defamation case.
item.content:encoded:
Some vehicles in Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s convoy met with an accident on the Purvanchal Expressway in Uttar Pradesh at around 10.15 am on Monday while he was travelling from Lucknow to Sultanpur for a court hearing in a defamation case, PTI reported.

Sultanpur Superintendent of Police Vineet Jaiswal said no one was injured, The Indian Express reported.

Media reports had initially said that several persons were injured.

Gandhi was travelling to Sultanpur to appear before a special MP-MLA court in connection with a 2018 defamation case for his remarks about Union Home Minister Amit Shah. He has been acquitted in the matter.

The incident occurred when a private vehicle at the front of the convoy, reportedly belonging to a Congress leader, applied the brakes suddenly for an unspecified reason, causing vehicles behind it to collide, a police officer told PTI.

The vehicles involved had joined the convoy midway. Congress workers from neighbouring districts were travelling in them.

The Uttar Pradesh Police has formed a special investigation team to probe what led to the accident and determine whether there were any lapses in security, escort arrangements or traffic management, PTI reported.

The team has been directed to investigate all aspects of the incident and submit a detailed report to police headquarters at the earliest.

item.content:encoded:
The Mumbai Police on Sunday detained at least 20 protesters during a demonstration at Chaityabhoomi in Dadar, demanding an investigation into the death of Indian Institute of Technology-Bombay student Sahil Wakode, The Hindu reported.

Sahil Wakode was found hanging in his hostel room on September 18. His family has alleged that he faced caste-based discrimination at the institute.

The protesters alleged that the police used force during the detentions, including manhandling women while removing them from Chaityabhoomi, the memorial and cremation site of BR Ambedkar, The Hindu reported.

The police said the gathering was unauthorised but did not respond to the protesters’ allegations of manhandling and misconduct.

Those detained were released from Tardeo, Worli and Dadar police stations after 8.30 pm.

Stand-up comedian Masoom Rajwani was among those detained. Rajwani shared a video of his detention on Instagram, showing police personnel taking him away from the protest site.

item.title: Rising pollution: India has dashboards to track problem – but not to track capability to solve it
item.description: Measuring policy outcomes has become more efficient than examining whether capability in providing public services has actually improved.
item.content:encoded:
On October 21, Delhi’s air quality slipped into the “poor” category, prompting the Commission for Air Quality Management to invoke Stage I of the Graded Response Action Plan across the National Capital Region.

This stage involves measures such as intensifying the mechanical sweeping roads and sprinkling water on them to keep the dust from rising. It also bans some kinds of construction and demolition activities.

As winter progresses, the air quality in the capital is likely to deteriorate further. Pollution-control measures will be activated, agencies will issue advisories, monitoring stations will track concentrations and dashboards will show the public how air quality is changing.

There is no shortage of information about Delhi’s air. A 2019 review of five emission-inventory studies by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water found that transport accounted for roughly 18% to 39% of PM2.5 emissions and road dust for 18% to 38%, while road dust alone accounted for 36% to 66% of PM10.

item.title: In a new book, Gopalkrishna Gandhi studies his grandfather Mahatma Gandhi’s views on Hinduism
item.description: ‘Whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.’
item.content:encoded:
“My religion teaches me that whenever there is distress which one cannot remove, one must fast and pray.”

India has had a tradition of fasting as a means of self-denial, self-purification, and self-mortification. This is an integral part of India’s religious and cultural history. Fasting on certain given days of the month and week, and on certain days connected with epic lore, such as on Mahashivaratri, makes fasts more than integral to Hinduism; it makes them vital and essential to it. In the Jaina tradition, fasting is even higher in the order of observances, as in Gandhi’s description of his Jain-influenced mother fasting unfailingly and cheerfully, having been seen earlier in this narrative. And Indian Muslims, of course, observe the annual fasts in the month of Ramzan punctiliously, Gandhi noting the practice with admiration in his illustrious colleague, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.

Gandhi himself belonged very squarely to that tradition, the reasons for his fasts varying, but the mode remaining very Hindu-Jaina, very religious in its DNA. item.title: When 11 women made a film together: ‘No weeping, no sad songs in the background’
item.description: The story of the collaboration behind the documentary ‘Mast Mahila Mandali’.
item.content:encoded:
There have been films with more than one directing credit. Then there is Mast Mahila Mandali (Cool Ladies Club), which has 11 directors.

Ten women came together under the supervision of an eleventh woman to point cameras at each other and have conversations about identity, ambition, desire and happiness. The result is a joyous and revelatory documentary about how women see themselves, and how they wish to be seen.

Shilpi Gulati, the film’s co-director, is a seasoned filmmaker (her credits include Naach Bhikhari Naach and Taala Te Kunjee) and academic.

The other women are first-time filmmakers. They are working-class residents of neighbourhoods in Mumbai’s M East municipal ward: Anjum Shaikh, Darshana Mayekar, Gauri Rane, Kavita Ghuge, Kavite Khomne, Nazneen Siddiqui, Rohini Kadam, Rehana Shaikh, Sheetal Navle and Vaishale Mane.

The story of how Gulati came to collaborate with associates of CORO India’s Right to Pee campaign is as fascinating as Mast Mahila Mandal itself. CORO India, a non-governmental organisation, has produced Mast Mahila Mandali.

The documentary assembles scenes of the women working, carrying out household chores and hanging out with each other. The feeling of sisterhood results in plenty of laughter as well as tears and regrets.

item.title: A new Brahmin-first party in UP symbolises a growing disquiet among BJP’s core voters
item.description: Some voters say they will pick the party best placed to defeat the BJP.
item.content:encoded:
Since February this year, an office space in Lucknow’s Sapru Marg has become the home of an audacious political experiment. Every day, a handful of men gather here and brainstorm how they can subvert the Bharatiya Janata Party in the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh.

Curiously, the men admit to having been BJP voters all their lives. They are mostly Brahmins, the privileged caste group that is a core constituency of the Hindutva party.

“The BJP was our party,” says Rajesh Shukla, a businessman who is a regular visitor here. “It has now been hijacked by backwards.”

The businessman was referring to other backward classes, or OBCs, a collection of castes that make up nearly half of UP’s population. Traditionally, the BJP has been seen as a party catering to upper-caste Hindus. Its earliest political architects like Deendayal Upadhyaya, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Murli Manohar Joshi were Brahmins from UP.

However, over the past decade, it has won two consecutive state elections after successfully wooing OBC and Scheduled Caste voters.

item.title: Why rats are on the ballot in Canada’s civic elections
item.description: Rodents point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.
item.content:encoded:
Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems. While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement.

Rats are ubiquitous urban residents that cities have attempted to evict for centuries. Often portrayed as dirty pests and bringers of plague, they can harbour pathogens that cause illnesses to people and pets, like rat bite fever and leptospirosis.

So why have cities had so little success in reducing rat numbers?

Well, rats are synanthropes, species that benefit from living alongside humans, and have adapted remarkably well to our paved, cacophonic and bustling streets. Cities provide abundant resources for rats to thrive: food scraps are meals; standing water on sidewalks supplies drinking water; and cracks in buildings offer access to shelter.

Municipal policies and bylaws shape how these environments are built and maintained, influencing living conditions for both people and rats. Thinking about rats through municipal elections can offer a more tangible way to understand how complex it is to manage rats without addressing broader issues.

item.title: ‘Switzy’: In her new novel Emma Cline inhabits a man with dementia
item.description: ‘Switzy’ raises a difficult question: if life remains meaningful even in the face of decline, what exactly justifies bringing it to an end?
item.content:encoded:
Emma Cline is best known as the author of novels about troubled young women. The Girls, her debut, inhabited a follower of a Charles Manson figure, who opted out of the murders at the last minute. Her second, The Guest, followed a callow beauty who’d attached herself to a wealthy man for accommodation.

Switzy, her third novel, longlisted for this year’s Booker Prize, turns to a different kind of protagonist. The novel follows an elderly American man making a final journey to Switzerland. The way to Golgotha? A last hurrah? Readers can quickly guess Switzerland is the place where David Hastings, our narrator, plans to end his life before his accelerating Alzheimer’s disease robs him of total agency.

Rather than scrutinising the ethics of such a decision, Cline focuses on the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves, how we construct our own version of events, and what happens when our ability to control that narrative begins to slip away.

David is not an immediately sympathetic guide. He is often curt, entitled and rude, particularly towards his assistant, Cody (who is not altogether warm). item.title: In Colombo, toilets are missing from urban development plans, putting women’s health at risk
item.description: Sri Lanka’s capital has a severe paucity of crucial public hygiene facilities, with women bearing the brunt of this neglect.
item.content:encoded:
“Menstruating monthly is not an illness,” says Sumithra Randenigala, who works as a security guard in Sri Lanka’s largest city, Colombo. But when she has her monthly period, the 26-year-old often calls in sick to work.

Getting her pay docked some days each month is a better alternative than being unable to use the toilet during the two-hour daily train commute from her sleepy seaside town Bentota to Colombo Fort Station.

“If I need to change my pad, the toilet on the train is locked or blocked. At work, guards aren’t allowed to use the office toilet,” she tells me at the Sri Lanka Tea Board, where she works.

She attended school till age 14, where she learnt about urinary tract infections in class. She knows the importance of changing her sanitary pad frequently. After several painful experiences of contracting UTIs, she now chooses to forfeit her daily pay sometimes, rather than risk an infection that would force her to take a week of unpaid sick leave.

What are the options for Sumithra and others like her who come into Colombo daily to work?

item.title: ‘I want readers to see our women rise to their full height’: Afghan novelist Nadia Hashmi
item.description: An interview with the author of ‘City of Widows’.
item.content:encoded:
Nadia Hashimi is an Afghan-American paediatrician and novelist who draws on her Afghan inheritance to write fiction for adults as well as young readers.

Her novels span generations and continents, taking on themes like forced migration, conflict, poverty, misogyny, colonialism, and addiction. Her books have been translated into as many as 17 languages. Her latest novel, City of Widows, focuses on women in the years since the Taliban regained power in Afghanistan.

An epic saga of an Afghan woman with secrets that threaten to undo the life she resurrected from ashes. She, a soldier in an elite military unit, and her musically gifted daughter find themselves at a crossroads of history.

Hashmi spoke to Scroll about her novel, the constant denial of education to women and girls and how the decades of conflict have shaped Afghan women and children and how fiction has changed perceptions about Afghanistan, moving away from its representation in the Western media.

item.title: Sunday book pick: The hard job of rehabilitation after civil conflict in Louise Kennedy’s ‘Stations’
item.description: The novel, published recently, looks at the immigrant experience of Irish youth in London in the 1980s.
item.content:encoded:
“And so they went on, throwing out truths without eye contact, the words so powerful neither of them could bear to behold their effect.”

In Louise Kennedy’s new novel, Stations, the Troubles in Northern Ireland are finally over.

The old enmity wants to be forgotten, but tension persists in everyday interactions. In Kennedy’s second novel, we witness the aftermath of long-drawn civil conflicts and how it lives on even after it is officially “over.” Stations deals with the hard job of rehabilitation of the self after such tragedies – especially the youth, who have already lost much and have much more to lose.

New to London

We witness the mass immigration from Ireland primarily to England, particularly to London. Young Irish men and women, with little education or skill, fled to the oppressor country for jobs, housing, or to simply run away from their painful histories. item.title: How the British looted Indian property after the uprising of 1857 – and justified it
item.description: In diaries and written accounts, English officers and wives cheer on the plunder of Indian belongings as retribution and revenge for violence by sepoys.
item.content:encoded:
Crockery from the Awadh palace. Silver items and animals from Nana Saheb Peshwa’s Bithur palace. Ornaments and silk garments belonging to Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. These were among the items looted by the British during the uprising of 1857.

But looting, it seems from books written by British men and women who experienced the rebellion, was only what violent Indians did. Their accounts present a rather different framing of the marauding. Their descriptions of the plunder by the British suggest that they were heroes who were merely rectifying an unfortunate mistake.

Even as they expressed a fear of their belongings falling into Indian hands, British writers also describe indulging in the plunder and destruction of Indian property and cheering it on – despite a proclamation from the East India Company authorities forbidding this.

They did so with impunity, fearing neither social ostracisation nor judicial repercussions.

‘All we valued was lost to us…’

When the uprising began in Meerut on May 10, 1857, the looting was incidental since the focus of the sepoys of the East India Company was to punish their British officers.

But Delhi, where the sepoys went next, witnessed large-scale looting.

“Delhi Police, sharam karo,” they shouted. Delhi Police, you should be ashamed.

item.title: Translation has several different relationships with time. AI does not get any of them
item.description: ‘AI may translate that word and save you the joy and misery of translation. That is not its strength. In fact, that is its danger.’
item.content:encoded:
These days I think a lot about translation and time. What might be the relation between the two, you may ask? Am I thinking of how much time it takes to translate something? Perhaps.

Although there is no standard time there, some take longer than some others and that may depend on how much “time” a translator has to how much “time” a particular text demands. I could think of the “time” in a text as when and in which time has an author situated her text – the narrative time.

Do I, as a translator, manage to capture the same narrative time, or does my modern idiom transpose the “time” of the text to another “time”?

For instance, the translator-historian Manu Devadevan recently mentioned on a panel that AK Ramanujan’s translation of Mahadeviakka and other women vacanakars made them sound like Sylvia Plath. item.title: ‘Hazrat Mahal’: Rosie Llewellyn-Jones’s book keeps the rebel begam at the edge of her own story
item.description: From an unknown identity to a death far from the land she fought for, Hazrat Mahal remains a footnote in her own story.
item.content:encoded:
History is read and reread, yet some parts always remain unexplored. Begam Hazrat Mahal is reintroduced by Rosie Llewellyn-Jones as the rebel begam of Awadh in Hazrat Mahal: The Rebel Begam of Awadh.

“Rebel” and “begam” are the two words that Hazrat Mahal epitomises. She embraced rebellion and royalty, but at the cost of her home and freedom. Llewellyn-Jones calls her “an elusive figure in Indian history”.

Reading Hazrat Mahal is a reminder that history written about men and women is not the same. Before Hazrat Mahal arrives at the centre of her own story, we encounter the men around her. The narrative establishes the king, the court and her son before she comes fully into view. For a book bearing her name, this delayed arrival is striking: we first come to know the world that contains her, and only later the woman who will come to challenge it.

What’s in a name?

But why are we exploring her through the men around her? This question was constantly on my mind as I read the biography. It may already seem surprising that she is even referred to as Mahal. item.title: Flashback: When CEC Lyngdoh refused BJP demand for early Gujarat poll until voter roll was updated
item.description: The Election Commission insisted on remedying the list since many voters, especially Muslims, had been displaced from their homes after the 2002 riots.

The deletion of nearly 13 crore names from the draft list as a result of the Special Intensive Revisions of electoral rolls under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has echoes of a controversy in Gujarat in 2002. The situation was similar, but the outcomes were different.

It was July 2002. Five months of sustained violence in the aftermath of the Godhra train burning in February that year had torn Gujarat apart. The post-Godhra attacks, largely on Muslims, had displaced thousands. Many had migrated from their homes and were living in relief camps.

In the middle of the mayhem, at 3 pm on July 19, Bharatiya Janata Party general secretary Arun Jaitley met with Chief Election Commissioner JM Lyngdoh. The chief election commissioner replied, “Gujarat is different because it is the case of a discredited government.” Jaitley accused him of using political language.

“Language of that kind is not a politician’s prerogative,” Lyngdoh countered. After all, there had to be an end to this sophistry, Lyngdoh writes in his book, Chronicle of an Impossible Election.

On October 25, Brazilians will return to the polls for the second round of the presidential election. The results will matter not only for the future of country itself, but also for the region and the world.

Alongside Canada and Mexico, Brazil, under the leadership of current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is one of the few countries in the region that has stood up to Donald Trump’s meddling and interference attempts.

The rise of the far right

Under Lula, Brazil still serves as a bulwark against the imposition of right-wing populist agendas critics say run counter to the broader interests of local societies, but cater to the interests of certain domestic elites. It is within this context that we must consider the Brazilian election alongside other electoral processes in the democratic world.

Many Trump-style leaders have recently come to power in the continent. The Economist compiled descriptive statistics to try to capture the trend. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro – son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro – would be the 12th. item.title: ‘Partita’: Barbara Kingsolver’s novel is about a musician bringing the rhythms of her life together
item.description: The novel is also a fascinating character study of women’s lives and relationships, and of changing American generations and traditions.
item.content:encoded:
A partita is a musical composition, often for a soloist. As Livia, the protagonist of Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel, Partita, explains to Sigurd, as they begin an all-consuming romance, it’s “made up of a lot of parts with different paces and moods. […] The parts are all different, and the artist’s work is to make them all add up to something that feels whole.”

Livia is just 20 at Indiana University, far from home, on a prestigious music scholarship. Distracted by the pursuit of excellence and the perfect love, she does not yet know that her life will be a partita, one she must make whole.

The contrasting parts of Livia’s life include three romantic relationships, an extraordinary piano talent, two bodily traumas, a fraught relationship with a violent, unloving mother, several losses, unspoken truths, loyal friends, and her brother’s suicide. The grief of losing her brother stifles Livia for decades. She focuses on piano virtuosity that takes her ever further from understanding herself – that is, until she is forced home.

item.title: In Goa, developers are grabbing eco-sensitive hilly land – ‘legally’
item.description: The state’s laws and curbs aimed at protecting the hills to prevent landslides are being systematically dismantled.

Right before the Mapusa river meets the Mandovi river near Panjim, it crosses the wetlands, creeks and low lying paddy fields of Salvador Do Mundo. Surrounding these large stretches of paddy fields are houses and forested hills with steep slopes. Telangana-based real-estate company, KGL Realtors Private Limited bought 20,000 square metres of land on one of these hills.

When the land was bought, the sale deed described it as “barren and waste land”. In Goa, a state-wide regional plan dictates what activities are permitted on a piece of land. The land that KGL bought is zoned as eco-sensitive land where development is regulated. It specifically categorises all of it as Natural Cover and part (4,000 square metres) of it as Natural Cover with “No Development Slopes”.

item.content:encoded:
Jamia Millia Islamia university on Saturday shifted all its classes online until further notice amid protests on campus demanding elections for the constitution of the students’ union, reported The Indian Express.

The announcement came soon after students alleged that the university administration had “attacked” those who have been on a hunger strike for 13 days and tried to dismantle the protest site.

As Wikipedia notes, Almora is a municipal town and cantonment in Uttarakhand’s Kumaun region. It did not emerge from the pressures of recent urbanisation. Rather, it is a 600-year-old town situated on the Kashyap Hills. It sits on a 5-km-long mountain ridge that forms a distinct horseshoe shape.

Indeed, Almora is older than Kolkata, Chennai or Mumbai.

During the late 16th century, the Chanda rulers of Kali Kumaon (today’s Champawat) shifted their capital to Almora, which, in certain accounts, was referred to as Alamnagar. This is how the town is believed to have been founded. It later passed into the hands of the Gorkhas for a brief period and became part of British India in 1816, following the formalisation of the Treaty of Sugauli between the British and the Gorkhas.

Beyond this ruler-oriented history, Almora has a rich past of its own. Hailed as the cultural capital of Kumaun, it encompasses linguistic, literary, and spiritual history that give it the life of a thriving town.

item.title: As memories become entangled with machines, who controls what we remember?
item.description: History could now be determined by algorithms.
item.content:encoded:
My phone chimed with an automated “memory” slideshow from an old trip, set to gentle music, the skies impossibly blue, the faces so bright. I watched it twice before realising what bothered me: I hadn’t chosen the photos, the order, or the mood. Something else had decreed what my holiday felt like. If the machine had the sky wrong, would I know? Is a memory still mine once something else has contrived it?

But how reliable are our memories anyway? Elizabeth Loftus, a pioneer in false memory research, proved decades ago that a single leading question can rewrite our recollections. Today, experts know that memory is actively rebuilt every time we remember.

The act of offloading memory onto external tools – like a simple notebook – blurs the line between the mind and the environment. This phenomenon, described as the “extended mind” by philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers, finds a modern parallel in media theory through the concepts of mediatisation and mediation, where historical reality is consumed in a pre-edited format.

Modern Europe was shaped by the 18th-century Enlightenment, which dreamt of reason and science, technology, democracy, national sovereignty, the free market, and a society based on individual rights and freedoms. Was the holocaust the great aberration of this dream? Believers in the Enlightenment idea – which continues to define modernity worldwide – would say so: a devastating violation.

item.title: A critical flaw in PHP, ‘backbone of the web’, has cyber experts scrambling for a fix
item.description: The incident shows that vulnerabilities will recur as long as the world treats open-source foundational tools charity rather than critical security investment.
item.content:encoded:
Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.

The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.

What is PHP?

PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.

The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.

Most problems that change the world don’t look like problems at all.

They look like mild inconveniences, the kind of thing most people shrug off and live with.

MP Ramachandran couldn’t shrug it off. He was obsessed with white clothes, wore only white shirts, washed them himself and was perpetually dissatisfied with the result. The whites faded, they yellowed, they looked like they’d given up. And every fabric whitener on the market made the problem worse rather than better.

Most people would have bought a different shirt.

Ramachandran built a company.


MP Ramachandran was not a typical entrepreneur. He was an accountant working in Mumbai who wore only white. His biggest frustration was that whites never stayed that way, they faded quickly, stains showed more easily and they looked old and ragged faster than coloured clothes.

That frustration became the catalyst.

Robin Blue was the dominant player in fabric whiteners at the time. But the problem with these powders was the process: consumers had to manually dissolve the powder, strain it through cloth and hope it didn’t leave blue patches on the fabric. item.title: Why India needs citizen-centric governance for everyday democracy
item.description: Significant effort is required to extract even basic accountability from the state.

In recent months, young Indians have felt compelled to petition, protest, run aggressive social media campaigns and push back against the government’s business-as-usual approach to irregularities in the manner in which electoral lists are being revised and in the way examinations are being conducted.

These protests reflect a wider frustration with the lack of avenues for citizens to engage with and hold accountable the governments and representatives they elect across levels.

Between the five-year election cycles, citizens have few systemic avenues to engage with their elected leaders and governments, contribute to decision-making, track commitments and projects or seek remedial action.

When the state fails to offer meaningful platforms for engagement and accountability, people are left with no options but to resort to protests on matters as basic as access to drinking water, quality education, health care or pothole-free roads or obstacle-free footpaths or fair examinations and recruitment to government services.

Parvati Nawar, a fish-seller from a presidency town, wrote a letter to the government of the British Raj in 1883 seeking protection from the police. She complained that the police were oppressing vendors at the local market.

Not only is it awe-inspiring that she stood up to the might of authority, but that she wrote her letter in a format colonial authorities couldn’t ignore or erase from their archives. item.title: What is the Socratic method? Could it be used to test students in the age of AI?
item.description: Classrooms should encourage and asses dialogue as opposed to purely descriptive assessments to assist a student’s learning.

In the humanities, where the whole aim is critical and creative reflection, educators face a thorny question. How do you develop and measure thinking of the kind that a machine could not genuinely imitate?

AI has proven it can answer questions well. But can it ask questions? And can it ask the right questions?

This is the philosophical method at the heart of the work of the Ancient Greek philosopher, Plato. His Socratic method of teaching is, perhaps, the mode of thinking we need to emulate in our teaching and learning today.

There is a dialogue for all the great philosophical questions: what justice is; what courage or love really requires; what makes a good friend; and even how we acquire knowledge.

item.title: Rejoinder: Use of Kafka’s cockroach metaphor for Dalit identity undermines anti-caste politics
item.description: The legacy of Dalit politics is resistance and defying dehumanisation.

In his article “Being a Dalit, being a cockroach: A self-reflective note on Kafka’s ‘Metamorphosis’”, Bhimraj M, a scholar at University of Oxford, uses an autobiographical lens and diagnoses his dalitness as a Kafkaesque condition. He compares his place in the caste society to that of Franz Kafka’s cockroach character Gregor Samsa.

As Dalit scholar-activists from Delhi University and Jawaharlal Nehru University we find this metaphor inappropriate, misleading and potentially regressive. Dalit consciousness, we argue, is fundamentally political, not existential and it requires analogies that foreground active resistance.

Bhimraj is admittedly comfortable in his “familiar” cockroach-ness, and detests being humanised. Yet, he yearns for and, eventually, resolves to seek a humanness for himself. “How am I supposed to feel when my fellow Dalit students are forced to clean bathrooms in schools, humiliated as ‘quotawallas’ or even driven to suicide in colleges?” he asks.

Enraged, we say! Such has been the approach of Dalit movement from Phule to Ambedkar and Kanshiram. The Dalit Panther movement of the 1970s sought to transform indignation into collective resistance, with “Panther” symbolising strength and defiance against oppression.

item.title: In Bengal, Christians allegedly assaulted by Bajrang Dal mob, forced to perform Hindu rituals
item.description: The minor girls of the families were threatened with rape and abduction, while the complainant was nearly disrobed, she told Scroll.
item.content:encoded:
Three Christian families in a village in West Bengal’s Paschim Medinipur District were harassed over three days, intimidated and forced to perform Hindu rituals by Bajrang Dal members, according to a first information report seen by Scroll.

The underage girls of the families were threatened with rape and abduction, while one woman was nearby disrobed, the family members told Scroll. The mob threatened to burn them alive and made repeated demands that they leave Christianity, they said.

No arrests have been made so far.

On October 18, around 3.30 pm, 40-year-old Laxmi Mondal was doing household chores when a mob of more than 10 people, including at least three women, barged into her home in Patlapur village.

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Wednesday announced that madrasas recognised as schools in the state would not have their weekly holiday on Friday, reported The Indian Express. Instead, they will be shut on Fridays.

In India, Islamic seminaries are called madrasas.

The weekly holiday in madrasas is typically on Friday, the day that Muslims usually participate in congregational prayers.

The government in July abolished its statutory madrasa board and brought educational institutions run by all six notified minority communities under a single regulatory authority.

Institutions run by Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains and Parsis are now regulated by the Uttarakhand State Authority for Minority Education, created after the 2025 Uttarakhand Minority Education Act came into force on July 1.

On Wednesday, Dhami said that the new rules on weekly holidays aim to bring minority-run institutions under common academic and administrative standards.

“We have already introduced a Uniform Civil Code in the state,” Dhami was quoted as saying. “There should be a uniform system for everyone. All educational institutions should operate in the same direction, and we are working towards that goal.”

The new rule will apply to madrassas that have been recognised by the education department and those that have applied for recognition, The Print reported.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Cashless Nation: How UPI Changed Everything’, by Santanu Paul and B Sambamurthy.
item.content:encoded:
UPI is a major agent of transformation, but seen through the prism of geography, prosperity and gender, it is the story of an uneven revolution. The adoption gap between rich and poor states, urban and rural regions, as well as men and women, remains substantial. Despite UPI’s relentless march across the length and breadth of the country, there are large swathes of the economy where cash still reigns supreme.

A handful of prosperous states serve as torchbearers for the revolution. Between April and June 2025, Maharashtra led with over 6 billion UPI transactions, nearly twice that of Karnataka, which came in shy of 4 billion. Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu followed. Four of these states are more industrialised and more prosperous. The exception is Uttar Pradesh, but it is a huge state in terms of population, so it records high transaction volumes in absolute terms. A look at state-wise per capita UPI usage further reveals that residents of richer states average about 13 UPI transactions per month. item.title: India asks citizens in France to exercise caution amid unrest
item.description: Demonstrations demanding education reforms have snowballed into wider protests in the European country.
item.content:encoded:
The Indian embassy in Paris on Wednesday issued an advisory asking Indian citizens to exercise caution amid violent protests in France.

Widespread demonstrations are being held in several European countries against increased cost of living, rising fuel prices and allegedly worsening public services.

In France, student-led protests that began in mid-September demanding education reforms have snowballed into a wider unrest. Some demonstrations have turned violent, with protesters targeting public buildings, looting luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacking police vehicles and officers.

On Tuesday, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said that new curfews will be imposed in parts of the country, as the authorities sought to restore order after weekend demonstrations turned into riots.

The authorities would coordinate with mayors to decide whether imposing a curfew was necessary in their respective provinces, Lecornu said.

In view of the curfews and the unrest, the Indian embassy advised citizens in France to be vigilant, avoid large gatherings and crowded places, and follow instructions from the local authorities.

Indians were also asked to stay informed through local news outlets and check for disruptions to public transport services.

On Monday, similar advisories were issued by the Indian embassies in Italy and Albania, where protests have also caused public disorder amid clashes with the police.
